title: How Bridges Carry Loads
summary: Every bridge solves one problem: moving weight sideways to solid ground. Explore the ideas, study the forces, challenge the myths and build a bridge of your own.

sources.title: A Brief History of Bridge Design

sections.title: Forces every bridge must handle
sections.summary: Compression pushes, tension pulls, and every part of a bridge is doing one of the two.
paragraphs: A bridge carries two kinds of load. The dead load is the bridge's own weight, which never goes away. The live load is everything that crosses it: people, vehicles, wind and snow.

Inside the structure, those loads become internal forces. Compression squeezes material together, like a stack of books being pressed down. Tension stretches material apart, like a rope in a tug of war.

Different materials are good at different jobs. Stone and concrete are strong in compression but weak in tension. Steel cables are excellent in tension but buckle when pushed. Good designs give each material the force it handles best.
Engineers also worry about shear, where one part of the structure slides past another, and torsion, a twisting force that wind can introduce on long spans.
keyPoints: Dead load is constant; live load changes.
Match each material to the force it resists best.

items.title: Beam
items.text: A horizontal span supported at both ends. Simple to build, but long beams sag unless they are deep or supported.

items.title: Arch
items.text: The curve turns downward load into compression that flows into the abutments at each end.

items.title: Truss
items.text: Triangles make a rigid frame. Each member is mostly in pure tension or pure compression.

items.title: Suspension
items.text: Deck loads hang from cables. The cables carry tension over towers into anchors on the shore.

sections.title: Challenge: is the arch always strongest?
sections.summary: Two common claims, tested against the physics.

items.title: Claim: arches never fail
points: Arches need solid abutments to resist sideways thrust.
A weak foundation lets the arch spread and collapse.

items.title: Claim: thicker is always safer
points: A heavier bridge may need bigger foundations.

items.a: Their light, flexible decks respond to wind. Designers add stiffening trusses and aerodynamic shapes to control movement.

items.q: Can a bridge be too strong?
items.a: Over-building costs money and materials, and stiff structures can crack where flexible ones would absorb movement.

sections.title: Build a craft-stick truss bridge
paragraphs: Build a small truss and test how much weight it carries before it bends. Record your results and try a second design.
materials: Two stacks of books as supports
A small bucket and coins as load
steps: Glue two sticks into a long beam and let them dry.
Add diagonal sticks to form triangles along both sides.
Rest the span across the books with 20 cm between supports.
Hang the bucket in the middle and add coins one at a time.
Record the load at which the bridge bends.
